title: Jurassic Coast Case Study

concepts.def: 95 mile World Heritage coastline in Dorset and East Devon.
Made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 for fossils and geology.
Chalk stacks at the eastern end formed by marine erosion.
Near-circular bay carved into folded limestone and clays.
Famous natural limestone arch west of Lulworth Cove.
Bring jobs but cause traffic, litter and path erosion. 🪨

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Jurassic Coast stretches ~95 miles.

It runs from Exmouth in East Devon to Studland Bay in Dorset.

Became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.

Lulworth Cove shows differential erosion.

Sea breached a hard Portland limestone band then scooped softer clay behind.

The harder chalk at the back stopped the bay growing further.

Tourism brings benefits and costs.

Roughly 14 million visits a year support jobs and shops.

But narrow lanes jam, paths erode and fossil hunting damages rare specimens.

mcqs.q: How do headlands and bays form on a discordant coastline?
options: Less resistant rock (e.g. clay) is eroded faster, forming bays; more resistant rock (e.g. chalk) is eroded slower, left protruding as headlands — perpendicular bands of geology.
Headlands and bays form because of differences in sea temperature.
Headlands form where the sea bends round to attack the land.
Constructive waves build sandcastles and destructive waves wash them away.

mcqs.q: What is the sequence of headland erosion from crack to stump?
options: Stacks form where rocks fall from the cliff into the sea.
Stacks form when the sea level rises and floods a hill.
Crack to cave to arch to stack to stump — waves widen cracks into caves, two caves meet to form an arch, the arch collapses leaving a stack, and the stack erodes to a stump.
Constructive waves build sandcastles and destructive waves wash them away.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between constructive and destructive waves?
options: Big waves are destructive and small waves are constructive.
Constructive waves build sandcastles and destructive waves wash them away.
Stacks form when the sea level rises and floods a hill.
Constructive waves have strong swash and weak backwash, building beaches; destructive waves have weak swash and strong backwash, dragging sediment offshore and eroding cliffs.
